Converging and Diverging Lenses

A lens is a transparent object whose curved surfaces refract light in a controlled way. A converging (convex) lens is thicker at the center and focuses parallel rays to a focal point \(F\) at a distance \(f\) (the focal length) from the lens. A diverging (concave) lens is thinner at the center and spreads parallel rays so they appear to originate from a focal point on the same side.

The power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length:

\[P = \frac{1}{f} \qquad \text{(units: diopters, D} = \text{m}^{-1}\text{)}\]

A shorter focal length means a more powerful lens — the light bends more sharply.

Ray Tracing

To locate the image formed by a thin lens, we trace three principal rays from the tip of the object:

  1. Parallel ray: Enters parallel to the optical axis → passes through \(F\) on the other side (converging) or appears to come from \(F\) on the same side (diverging).
  2. Central ray: Passes straight through the center of the lens — undeflected.
  3. Focal ray: Passes through \(F\) on the object side → exits parallel to the axis.

The intersection of any two of these rays locates the image.

The Thin Lens Equation

The relationship between object distance \(d_o\), image distance \(d_i\), and focal length \(f\) is:

\[\boxed{\frac{1}{d_o} + \frac{1}{d_i} = \frac{1}{f}}\]

The magnification relates image size to object size:

\[\boxed{M = \frac{h_i}{h_o} = -\frac{d_i}{d_o}}\]

A negative magnification means the image is inverted. A real image forms where light actually converges (\(d_i > 0\)) and can be projected onto a screen. A virtual image forms where light appears to diverge from (\(d_i < 0\)) and cannot be projected — you see it by looking through the lens.

Sign conventions:

Quantity Positive Negative
\(f\) Converging lens Diverging lens
\(d_o\) Object on incoming side (rarely used)
\(d_i\) Image on opposite side (real) Image on same side (virtual)
\(M\) Image upright Image inverted

Example: A Converging Lens

An object is placed 30.0 cm from a converging lens with \(f = 10.0\) cm.

\[\frac{1}{d_i} = \frac{1}{f} - \frac{1}{d_o} = \frac{1}{10.0} - \frac{1}{30.0} = \frac{3 - 1}{30.0} = \frac{2}{30.0}\]

\[d_i = 15.0\ \text{cm} \qquad M = -\frac{15.0}{30.0} = -0.500\]

The image is real (positive \(d_i\)), inverted (negative \(M\)), and half the size of the object. This is how a camera forms an image on its sensor.

Example: The Magnifying Glass

Now place the same object at \(d_o = 5.00\) cm — inside the focal length (\(d_o < f\)):

\[\frac{1}{d_i} = \frac{1}{10.0} - \frac{1}{5.00} = \frac{1 - 2}{10.0} = -\frac{1}{10.0}\]

\[d_i = -10.0\ \text{cm} \qquad M = -\frac{-10.0}{5.00} = +2.00\]

The image distance is negative — the image forms on the same side as the object. It is virtual (cannot be projected), upright (positive \(M\)), and magnified (\(|M| > 1\)). This is exactly what happens when you hold a magnifying glass close to a small object. The lens produces an enlarged virtual image that your eye perceives as being behind the lens.

The same equation, the same lens — but placing the object inside \(f\) versus outside \(f\) produces qualitatively different physics: real/inverted/reduced versus virtual/upright/magnified.

For a diverging lens (\(f < 0\)), the thin lens equation always yields \(d_i < 0\) regardless of object placement — the image is always virtual, upright, and reduced. A diverging lens cannot form a real image on its own.

*Personal note: The thin lens equation \(1/d_o + 1/d_i = 1/f\) has a structural cousin in Chapter 25: the series capacitor equation \(1/C_\text{eq} = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2\). Both are reciprocal sums. Both combine two quantities (distances or capacitances) into a third. And in both cases, the “equivalent” result is always smaller than either individual value when both terms are positive. This pattern — reciprocal addition — recurs whenever two elements share the same throughput (charge for series capacitors, light rays for the lens). It is not a coincidence.

*Personal note: The human eye is the most sophisticated lens system in nature. The cornea provides roughly two-thirds of the eye’s optical power, with the lens contributing the rest. Together they project a real, inverted image onto the retina, where roughly 120 million rods (sensitive to brightness) and 6 million cones (sensitive to color) convert light into neural signals. The brain flips the image upright. What no simple glass lens can do is accommodate — the ciliary muscles change the lens shape to adjust focal length in real time, shifting focus from near to far objects in milliseconds. When this system fails, we correct it with external lenses: a diverging lens for myopia (nearsightedness, where the focal length is too short) and a converging lens for hyperopia (farsightedness, where the focal length is too long).
